note: Summaries in our own words for study. Always check the College's current version before using in practice.

guidance.title: The routine eye examination
points: By law the sight test must include whatever checks are needed to spot injury, disease or abnormality of the eye or elsewhere, not just the refraction.
Beyond that legal minimum, you decide what the exam includes using your professional judgement.
Record every clinical finding and explain your findings and advice to the patient.
How often someone is seen depends on their clinical needs, with recommended minimum intervals.
You can never make buying glasses a condition of having the eye test.

guidance.title: The needs-led examination
points: A needs-led exam is for a patient who doesn't need a legal sight test, for example someone with a specific problem.
The law doesn't restrict who can carry one out.
The tests you do must match the reason the patient came in.

guidance.title: The domiciliary eye examination
points: Home visits are for people who can't get to a practice because of physical or mental disability.
Only offer one when the patient, a relative or main carer asks for it.
Bring suitable portable equipment and adapt your techniques to the setting.
Care homes bring extra things to think about, such as consent and communicating with staff.

guidance.title: Patients who present as an emergency
points: Use your judgement to decide the best action in the patient's interests.
If you see them, make clear it's an emergency assessment of their symptoms, not a full sight test.
If you don't see them, send them to the right professional and say how urgently.
All practice staff should know the protocol for walk-in emergencies.

guidance.title: Flashes and floaters
points: Refer to a colleague if you aren't competent to assess the patient yourself.
Follow local protocols for managing and referring these patients.
The College urgency table lists floaters or flashes under 48 hours with tobacco dust as an emergency within 24 hours.

guidance.title: Patients at risk from glaucoma
points: Do the relevant tests whenever a patient is in an at-risk group.
Higher-risk groups include people over 40, first-degree relatives of someone with glaucoma, and some ethnic groups.
In England, an IOP of 24 mmHg or more should be treated (in line with NICE).
Follow local protocols if you work in a community glaucoma service.

guidance.title: Patients with diabetes
points: Take reasonable care to look for diabetic eye changes.
Encourage every patient with diabetes to attend the NHS diabetic eye screening programme; your exam doesn't replace it.

guidance.title: Patients who drive
points: The DVLA (or DVA in Northern Ireland) sets the vision standards and decides whether someone is fit to drive.
It's the patient's legal duty to tell the DVLA about a condition that could affect driving.
If they don't meet the standard, advise them not to drive.
If they keep driving and you can't persuade them to stop, you should tell the DVLA and let the patient know you're doing so.
Give advice on tints, which matter for driving.
There's no legal eyesight standard for mobility scooters or powered wheelchairs, but the DVLA recommends one.

guidance.title: Display screen (computer) users
points: Screen users are entitled to vision screening or a full eye exam; a full exam is in their best interests.
Employers only have to pay for glasses needed specifically for screen work, not general-purpose ones that also cover it.

guidance.title: Examining younger children
points: The child's care is your first concern, even when they're too young to consent themselves.
Assess vision, eye muscle balance, binocular function, refractive error and eye health.
Don't refuse a patient because of age alone; refer or transfer care if a specialist would be better.
Build rapport with the child and talk to them and their adult appropriately.
Protect yourself against unfounded allegations, and make clear school screening isn't a full eye exam.

guidance.title: Children with myopia
points: Keep up to date with the evidence on myopia management.
Be able to explain myopia and the options for managing it.
Recommend myopia management when it's clinically indicated and in the child's best interests.
Get, and record, explicit consent before starting a myopia management treatment.

guidance.title: Binocular vision anomalies
points: Binocular vision assessment is a normal part of every exam, using acuity tests suited to the patient's age.
Know the treatment options for binocular vision anomalies.
Only manage patching if your knowledge and skills are up to date.
When you refer for orthoptic or amblyopia treatment, tell the patient what treatment is likely.
Share information with other professionals involved in community care.

guidance.title: Patients with low vision
points: People don't have to be registered sight impaired to benefit from low vision services.
Assess each patient by their needs and follow local protocols.
Think about emotional support and social care, not just magnifiers.
Low vision care is multidisciplinary and rarely a one-off.
Refer if you lack the expertise.
Glasses or contact lenses for registered sight-impaired patients must be supplied by, or supervised by, an optometrist, dispensing optician or doctor.

guidance.title: Patients with a disability
points: You must make reasonable adjustments.
Speak to the patient directly, not to their companion.
Don't assume a physical disability means a learning disability.
It's fine to ask what caused the disability and whether it's permanent.
Be flexible with techniques and note what worked for next time.

guidance.title: Autistic patients
points: Offer a visit before the appointment so the setting feels familiar.
Book a quiet time with little waiting.
Explain each step in advance in clear language with direct instructions.
Allow extra time.

guidance.title: Patients with dementia or cognitive impairment
points: These patients may have extra eye conditions.
Adapt your techniques as needed.
Follow the consent guidance when discussing them with relatives or carers; capacity law differs across the UK nations.
Only prescribe glasses when it's in the patient's best interests.

guidance.title: Patients with learning disabilities
points: They may have extra eye conditions and other health problems.
Choose tests that suit the patient.
Talk to the patient directly rather than to their carer.
Plan adjustments in advance with the patient and carer where possible.
Give a written report as well as a verbal one.

guidance.title: Specific learning difficulties (e.g. dyslexia)
points: Investigate visual problems with a thorough eye exam using suitable tests.
Tell patients there's currently no strong evidence that coloured lenses improve visual function, though some report finding them helpful.

guidance.title: Patient records
points: Full, accurate, clear records made at the time are essential for care, continuity and your own protection if there's a complaint.
Records belong to the practice where they were made.
Electronic records need security, backups, training, a continuity plan and safe disposal of old equipment.
Images must be dated, linked to the right patient and given enough time to be analysed.
Keep records confidential and follow the Data Protection Act 2018 and GDPR.
Patients have a right to see their records.

guidance.title: Prescribing spectacles
points: After any sight test you must give a prescription, or a statement that none is needed, straight away.
If there's no significant change, still give the prescription with a note saying so.
Only prescribe or recommend new glasses when it's in the patient's interests.
If you make a small change, be clear about the benefit and record your reasoning and advice.
The PD isn't part of the prescription.

guidance.title: Sale and supply of spectacles
points: Unregistered staff selling to restricted groups (e.g. children, sight-impaired people) must be supervised, and you must be on the premises at key stages.
Make sure the glasses meet the patient's needs and explain their use and care.
Arrange reasonable aftercare.
Online or remote supply follows the same rules as in person.
Only make up prescriptions over two years old if it's in the patient's interests.
Patients can take their prescription anywhere.

guidance.title: Fitting contact lenses
points: Only registered optometrists, doctors, contact lens opticians, or supervised trainees can fit lenses.
Avoid fitting only occasionally; keep skills current.
Give zero-powered (cosmetic) lens wearers the same care as powered ones: the risks are the same.
Powered lens wearers need a sight test within the last two years (or sooner if the prescription says).
Record everything relevant and give written wear-and-care advice.
Don't fit lenses on yourself.

guidance.title: Contact lens specification
points: Once fitting is complete you must give a written specification for powered lenses, and should for zero-powered ones.
It must include an expiry date, which you set using your judgement.
Lenses can't be supplied after the specification expires.
Patients can buy lenses from any supplier, as long as a registrant oversees the sale.
If a supplier asks you to verify a specification, you need the patient's consent to share anything else.

guidance.title: Contact lens supply
points: Never supply powered lenses without a valid specification.
Powered lenses can be supplied directly, under supervision or under general direction.
Zero-powered lenses can be supplied directly or under supervision, but not under general direction.
Arrange reasonable aftercare for anyone you supply.

guidance.title: Contact lens check-ups
points: Carry out all key assessments, record them and tell the patient what you found.
Powered and zero-powered lens wearers get the same standard of care.
Set check-up frequency by the patient's clinical risk.
If you reissue a specification, you're responsible for it and should check the lenses being worn.

guidance.title: Contact lenses for overnight wear
points: Tell patients that sleeping in lenses raises their risk of complications.
See overnight wearers more often.

guidance.title: Contact lens equipment
points: Have suitable equipment and the skills to use it.
Have it verified and calibrated regularly.

guidance.title: Use and supply of drugs
points: Follow the law on using and supplying medicines in practice.
Know the indications, cautions, contraindications and side effects of anything you use; take extra care with at-risk groups.
Tell patients how to use a drug and what to do if they react; if you're unavailable, they should go to A&E.
You can delegate instilling drops, but you stay responsible.
Don't treat or write POM orders for yourself or people close to you, except minor ailments or emergencies.
Store drugs as the manufacturer says and report adverse reactions (Yellow Card).

guidance.title: Remote consultations
points: Use your judgement on whether remote care is in the patient's interests.
It needs a clinical governance framework so outcomes match in-person care and can be audited.
In a remote sight test, one optometrist stays responsible for the refraction, health check and prescription.
Triage patients first, including their digital access and skills.

guidance.title: Developing knowledge and skills
points: Keep up to date with the law, GOC standards, College guidance and developments in practice.
Review your own work regularly and stay within your competence.
Meet the GOC's continuing education requirements; the College encourages going further.

guidance.title: Protecting patients from harm (raising concerns)
points: You must raise concerns about patient safety, including a colleague's fitness to practise. This is also called whistleblowing.
The law can protect you when you raise a genuine concern.
Act quickly, keep a record and protect patient confidentiality.
Log adverse incidents centrally (practice system or Accident Book) and report near misses for NHS patients to the right body.

guidance.title: Infection control
points: Infections spread person to person or via contaminated objects.
Provide a safe environment and follow infection control, including hand hygiene.
Keep your immunisations up to date.
Decontaminate equipment that touches patients and dispose of sharps and waste safely.
Know what to do after an accident, and use extra precautions for transmissible infections.

guidance.title: Health and safety on the premises
points: Follow health and safety law and keep the practice clean and safe.
Follow workplace safety procedures, report adverse incidents and take part in clinical audit.
Use routine infection control, and extra precautions when public health teams flag a concern.

guidance.title: Safeguarding children and adults at risk
points: Follow the optical sector's safeguarding guidance (from the Optical Confederation, now hosted by FODO).
Know your local procedure for reporting a safeguarding concern.

guidance.title: Consent
points: Patients have the right to be fully involved in decisions about their care; get consent before examining or treating someone with capacity.
Consent can be spoken, written or implied (e.g. resting on the chin rest after you explain). Going along with something they don't understand isn't consent.
Implied consent usually covers routine non-invasive tests. Get explicit consent for drops, contact lens fitting and contact tonometry.
People over 16 are presumed to have capacity. Capacity law is the Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England and Wales), the Adults with Incapacity Act 2000 (Scotland) and the Mental Capacity Act 2016 (NI).
Involve children and young people in decisions and encourage them to involve their parents; the law for under-16s differs across the UK.

guidance.title: Confidentiality
points: You, and anyone you employ, must protect patient information.
You may disclose it when the law requires it, or to prevent serious harm to the patient or others.
Limited sharing with others caring for the patient is allowed; anything else needs consent.
Anonymise where you can and guard against accidental disclosure.
For a child, you need their or their parents' consent unless it's in their best interests or they're at serious risk.
Confidentiality continues after death, with some exceptions such as a court order.

guidance.title: Partnership with patients
points: The patient's care is your first concern.
Explain things in a way they understand and tell them what to expect.
Respect their dignity, privacy, views and choices.
Help them make informed decisions.

guidance.title: Working with colleagues
points: Communicate well with colleagues, treat them fairly and act fast if a colleague puts patients at risk.
Only delegate to people with the right skills, tell the patient, and remember you stay responsible.
Referral letters should give the condition, the reason and the urgency; give the patient a copy and tell them what happens next.
Judge urgency using College guidance or local protocols.
Only registered people can do the protected functions of sight testing and contact lens fitting.

guidance.title: Dealing with complaints
points: Handle complaints sensitively and quickly, and be candid when things have gone wrong.
Don't treat a patient worse because they complained.
NHS contractors must have a complaints procedure; extend it to private patients.
Try to resolve complaints in practice; the Optical Consumer Complaints Service (OCCS) can help.

guidance.title: Maintaining boundaries
points: You're in a position of trust and must not abuse it.
Sexual or inappropriate emotional relationships with current or former patients are likely to cross the line.
Ask a colleague or professional body if you're unsure.
Warn colleagues about unprofessional behaviour and report it if patients are at risk.

guidance.title: Social media and online behaviour
points: Keep the same professional standards online.
Never share patient information; staying anonymous online is harder than it seems.
Copyright and defamation law apply to your posts.
Declare conflicts of interest when posting professionally.

guidance.title: Honesty and integrity
points: Be honest and trustworthy, and put patients first.
Don't discriminate against patients or colleagues.
Tell the GOC about anything that might affect your fitness to practise, and declare convictions, cautions and disciplinary action (except minor road traffic offences).
Co-operate with inquiries, hearings and complaints.
Don't accept gifts or inducements that could look like they affect your care, and be honest in money matters.
Have proper insurance throughout your registration.

guidance.title: Research and audit
points: Patient care and safety come first.
Get ethical approval for research on people or animals.
Work within the relevant law.

levels: Urgent: phone the eye department to triage

cells: Painful eye under 2 months after surgery (hypopyon, blebitis, endophthalmitis)
HZO with acute skin lesions (GP same day for antivirals; urgent eye referral if deeper cornea involved)
Corneal foreign body embedded in stroma or with a rust ring (unless trained to remove)
Acute dacryocystitis in children, or severe in adults
AKC with corneal macro-erosion or plaque
Dry eye with suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome or cicatricial pemphigoid
VKC with active limbal or corneal involvement
Sudden complete loss of vision under 6 hours
Sudden loss of vision of unknown cause, under 24 hours
Sudden change in vision under 2 weeks
Retinal detachment with the macula on
Flashes or floaters under 48 hours with tobacco dust
Retinal detachment with the macula off
CRVO with raised IOP (40 mmHg or more is an emergency)
Non-emergency retinal detachment (unless long-standing and symptom-free)
Severe eye pain with nausea or vomiting
New or worsening diplopia, squint, ptosis or nerve palsy
IOP 40 mmHg or more, whatever the cause
Sudden severe eye pain, or within 2 weeks of surgery

cmgs.title: Abnormalities of the pupil
cmgs.summary: Includes physiological anisocoria (about 1 in 5 people), Adie's tonic pupil, Horner's syndrome (small pupil, ptosis, no sweating on that side) and Argyll Robertson pupils (small, no light reaction, but constrict for near; late syphilis).
points: Explain harmless findings, or refer to ophthalmology or neurology if tests are needed.
cmgs.refer: New pupil defects: urgent. Painful Horner's: emergency within 24 hours.

cmgs.title: Acanthamoeba keratitis
cmgs.summary: A serious corneal infection, mostly in contact lens wearers exposed to water. The organism forms hardy cysts that are hard to kill.
points: Early: discomfort, redness, light sensitivity. Later: severe pain out of proportion to signs as nerves are involved.
Prevention: never let tap water touch lenses or cases.
Stop lens wear and refer as an emergency.
Treated with intensive drops for months; scarring may need a transplant.

cmgs.title: Anterior uveitis (iritis)
cmgs.summary: Inflammation at the front of the uvea with dull ache, redness, photophobia and blur, usually one eye. About half are idiopathic; many are HLA-B27 positive (linked to ankylosing spondylitis, IBD, sarcoidosis).
points: A third recur.
Uncomplicated cases: steroid drops plus a cycloplegic, with early review.
Refer urgently if there's no improvement within a week, or straight away if vision, IOP or the back of the eye is affected.
cmgs.refer: Annex 4 lists iritis as an emergency within 24 hours; the CMG lets suitably skilled optometrists start treatment in uncomplicated cases.

cmgs.title: Atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC)
cmgs.summary: A chronic allergic disease of the lids and ocular surface in people with atopic eczema.
points: Needs long-term treatment to prevent corneal scarring.
Early: anti-allergy drops and cool compresses. Severe: steroid courses; ciclosporin or tacrolimus if steroid-dependent.
Often co-managed by ophthalmology.

cmgs.title: Basal cell carcinoma (periocular)
cmgs.summary: The commonest malignant skin tumour in white people; around the eye it's typically a small, hard, pearly nodule on the lower lid. It grows slowly and rarely spreads.
points: Risk rises with UV exposure and outdoor work.
It must be told apart from benign lid lumps; biopsy confirms the diagnosis.
Treated by surgery (sometimes Mohs micrographic surgery) or radiotherapy.

cmgs.title: Blepharitis (lid margin disease)
cmgs.summary: Long-term inflammation of the lid margins. Anterior blepharitis affects the lash bases; posterior blepharitis is usually meibomian gland dysfunction. Bacteria or Demodex mites are usual causes.
points: Symptoms are irritation, though some people have none.
Regular lid hygiene is the mainstay for both types.
Topical antibiotics, or occasionally oral ones, can reduce symptoms and bacteria.
No treatment reliably cures it, so ongoing care is often needed.

cmgs.title: Blunt trauma
cmgs.summary: A forceful impact to the eye or orbit, from a black eye to orbital fractures, hyphaema, raised IOP or retinal damage.
points: Mild bruising settles with pain relief.
Look for fractures (restricted gaze, displaced eye) and internal damage.

cmgs.title: Chalazion (meibomian cyst)
cmgs.summary: A firm lump in the lid from a blocked meibomian gland opening.
points: Usually settles with warm compresses and massage.
If it persists: steroid injection or minor surgery under local anaesthetic.

cmgs.title: Chemical injury
cmgs.summary: Alkalis (e.g. oven and drain cleaners, ammonia) are worst because they penetrate the eye; acids, detergents, solvents and sprays also cause harm.
points: Irrigate immediately: sterile saline, or tap water if that's all there is, for at least 20 minutes.
Assess quickly, irrigate again, then same-day ophthalmology.
cmgs.refer: Emergency, as soon as possible (irrigate first).

cmgs.title: Concretions
cmgs.summary: Small white-yellow deposits on the tarsal conjunctiva, usually harmless.
points: If they cause irritation, they can be removed with a needle under topical anaesthetic.
Rarely need referral.

cmgs.title: Conjunctival pigmented lesions
cmgs.summary: Brown conjunctival lesions: racial melanosis, primary acquired melanosis (PAM), congenital melanocytosis, naevi (commonest) and rarely melanoma.
points: Mild racial melanosis needs no referral.
Others are monitored or referred routinely or urgently depending on the features.
Melanoma is treated surgically and recurs often.

cmgs.title: Conjunctival scarring
cmgs.summary: Scarring from injury, infection, allergy or autoimmune disease; trachoma is a major cause worldwide.
points: Scarred conjunctiva holds tears poorly, so dry eye symptoms are common.
Lubricants for mild cases; lid surgery or amniotic membrane grafts for severe.
cmgs.refer: Suspected Stevens-Johnson syndrome or cicatricial pemphigoid: urgent.

cmgs.title: Conjunctivitis (acute allergic)
cmgs.summary: A sudden allergic reaction (e.g. to grass pollen or animal fur) with itchy, red, swollen lids and conjunctiva.
points: Most settle within hours without treatment.
Anti-allergy drops help symptoms and recurrent episodes.

cmgs.title: Conjunctivitis (bacterial)
cmgs.summary: Red, sticky, watery eye(s) with discomfort but not pain. Usually clears in a few days; it's contagious.
points: Hygiene advice: don't share towels.
Antibiotic drops or ointment can speed recovery, though evidence of benefit in mild cases is limited.

cmgs.title: Conjunctivitis (chlamydial)
cmgs.summary: A sexually transmitted infection causing irritation, swelling and discharge, usually in one eye; most also have a genital infection.
points: Refer so they can have full STI testing via a sexual health (GUM) clinic.
Antibiotics are effective; partners may need treatment too.
cmgs.refer: Urgent, via the GP or eye department.

cmgs.title: Conjunctivitis (viral, non-herpetic)
cmgs.summary: Usually adenovirus. Red, uncomfortable eye(s); very contagious and self-limiting.
points: Antibiotics don't work and there's no effective antiviral.
Cool compresses and lubricants; no contact lenses during the acute phase.
Corneal opacities (subepithelial infiltrates) or severe inflammation may need steroid drops.

cmgs.title: Conjunctivitis medicamentosa
cmgs.summary: An irritant or allergic reaction to drops, ointments, contact lens solutions or cosmetics, often from preservatives. Redness, stinging and lid swelling.
points: Stop the cause and substitute if needed; preservative-free versions often solve it.

cmgs.title: Contact lens papillary conjunctivitis (CLAPC/GPC)
cmgs.summary: Inflammation of the upper tarsal conjunctiva in lens or prosthesis wearers, with papillae, redness, itch and mucus; it can make people give up lenses.
points: First: better lens hygiene, refit, and more frequent replacement (e.g. daily disposables).
Antihistamine or mast-cell-stabiliser drops.
Short steroid courses for severe cases.

cmgs.title: Contact lens-associated infiltrative keratitis
cmgs.summary: A sterile inflammatory reaction to bacteria on the lens, giving small peripheral infiltrates, redness and mild discomfort.
points: The key task is to tell it apart from microbial keratitis, which is an emergency.
Stopping lens wear usually settles it within 48 hours.
Reinforce lens hygiene: hand washing, replacing cases, no overnight wear.

cmgs.title: Corneal abrasion
cmgs.summary: A scratch to the corneal epithelium (fingernail, mascara brush, contact lens, trapped debris). Very painful.
points: Stains with fluorescein.
Antibiotic and/or lubricant drops depending on size and type; a cycloplegic can ease pain.
Refer if deep, contaminated or possibly infected.

cmgs.title: Corneal foreign body
cmgs.summary: Debris stuck to the cornea, often high-speed (grinding, hammering, DIY).
points: Remove under topical anaesthetic; remove any rust ring from iron particles.
Antibiotic cover if infection is likely.
Refer if it has penetrated deeper or may scar.
cmgs.refer: Embedded in the stroma or with a rust ring you can't remove: emergency within 24 hours.

cmgs.title: Corneal hydrops
cmgs.summary: In keratoconus, a split in Descemet's membrane floods the cornea with aqueous, making it suddenly cloudy.
points: Usually clears over 2–4 months.
No contact lenses during recovery; they may need refitting afterwards.
Refer quickly if complications such as new vessels appear.

cmgs.title: Corneal transplant rejection
cmgs.summary: The immune system attacks a corneal graft, causing pain, redness, blur and watering. Endothelial rejection threatens the graft.
points: Catch it early: intensive steroids can reverse it.

cmgs.title: Dacryocystitis (acute)
cmgs.summary: A bacterial infection of the tear sac, usually behind a blocked nasolacrimal duct. Sudden pain, redness and swelling at the inner corner, sometimes with fever.
points: Commonest in babies and in women over 40.
Distinguish it from orbital cellulitis; children go to hospital the same day.
Treated with antibiotics (sometimes IV) and drainage.
cmgs.refer: Children or severe: emergency within 24 hours. Mild in adults: urgent.

cmgs.title: Dacryocystitis (chronic)
cmgs.summary: Low-grade tear sac inflammation from a blocked duct, with watering and swelling at the inner corner. Pressing the sac may push mucus out of the puncta.
points: Warm compresses and massage; antibiotic drops for flare-ups.
Imaging helps plan surgery; a DCR makes a new route from the sac into the nose.

cmgs.title: Dry eye disease
cmgs.summary: Too few tears or poor-quality tears (aqueous deficiency or evaporation, often from MGD). Common with age, some drugs, inflammation, surgery or lid problems.
points: Grittiness, foreign-body feeling, discharge and blur, worse in wind or smoke.
Lubricants, screen breaks, blinking, hydration, avoiding dry or smoky air.
Punctal plugs or surgery to keep tears in.
Treat the lids when MGD is the cause.

cmgs.title: Ectropion
cmgs.summary: The lid (usually lower) sags away from the eye, mostly from age-related laxity, leaving a sore, red, watery eye.
points: Lubricating drops and ointment.
Tape the lid at night if it doesn't close; a bandage lens can protect the surface.
Surgery under local anaesthetic if these don't help.

cmgs.title: Entropion
cmgs.summary: The lid margin (usually lower) rolls in so lashes rub the eye. Usually age-related laxity, but scarring and trachoma also cause it.
points: Irritable, red, watery eye; vision may blur.
Temporary relief: taping the lid to the cheek, removing lashes, a bandage lens, lubricants.
These don't cure it, so routine referral for surgery is common.

cmgs.title: Episcleritis
cmgs.summary: Inflammation of the episclera with redness and mild aching; vision is unaffected. Most cases are idiopathic, about a third linked to systemic disease (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis, IBD).
points: Usually settles in 7–10 days but can recur.
Cold compresses and lubricants; steroid drops or oral anti-inflammatories if more severe.
Consider referral after a second recurrence.

cmgs.title: Facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy)
cmgs.summary: Weakness of the facial nerve, often Bell's palsy, so the lids may not close and the cornea dries out.
points: New cases go the same day to the GP or eye department: oral steroids work best within 72 hours.
Lubricant drops by day and ointment at night; tape the lids closed at night if needed.
Check for corneal drying and reduced sensation.

cmgs.title: Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy
cmgs.summary: An inherited, slowly progressive loss of endothelial cells in both eyes, so the cornea swells and vision becomes hazy (often worse in the morning).
points: Later, epithelial blisters can burst and hurt.
No cure; lubricants for comfort.
Affects cataract surgery planning.
Corneal transplant (often endothelial keratoplasty) if vision or comfort is poor.

cmgs.title: Herpes simplex keratitis
cmgs.summary: Reactivation of latent HSV-1 in the trigeminal nerve, causing corneal infection; the classic sign is a branching dendritic ulcer. Usually one eye; recurrences can scar.
points: A new epithelial-only case: topical antiviral.
Children, contact lens wearers and both-eye cases go to ophthalmology the same day.
If a recurrence hasn't improved after a week of antiviral, refer urgently.
Severe scarring may need a corneal transplant.

cmgs.title: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus
cmgs.summary: Shingles in the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve, from reactivated varicella zoster virus. A painful one-sided forehead rash that can involve the eye.
points: Rash involving the nose tip (Hutchinson's sign) raises the risk of eye involvement.
Oral antivirals from the GP, ideally within 72 hours of the rash.
cmgs.refer: Acute skin lesions: GP within 24 hours for antivirals; urgent eye referral if deeper cornea is involved.

cmgs.title: Hordeolum (stye)
cmgs.summary: An acute bacterial infection of a lid gland, giving a red, tender swelling. External = lash glands (stye); internal = meibomian gland.
points: Warm compresses relieve symptoms.
Topical antibiotics sometimes speed recovery; oral antibiotics if the infection is severe.

cmgs.title: Idiopathic epiretinal membrane
cmgs.summary: A thin membrane on the macular surface, affecting about 7% of older people. It may be harmless or contract and cause distortion and blur.
points: OCT confirms it.
Monitor if there are no symptoms.
Refer if vision is affected; surgery is vitrectomy with membrane peel.

cmgs.title: Marginal keratitis
cmgs.summary: An inflammatory (not infective) reaction to staphylococcal toxins from the lid margin, giving a peripheral infiltrate or shallow ulcer with a clear gap from the limbus.
points: Red, watery, painful eye.
Settles by itself, faster with steroid-antibiotic drops.
Treat the underlying blepharitis; sunglasses for light sensitivity.

cmgs.title: Microbial keratitis (bacterial, fungal)
cmgs.summary: Infection of the cornea, most often linked to contact lenses; also exposure, reduced sensation, injury, surgery, dry eye or immunosuppression.
points: Sudden pain, redness, discharge, photophobia and blur; a white infiltrate, often with an epithelial defect.
A sight-threatening emergency. Small low-risk ulcers may be started on antibiotics by the optometrist; most go the same day to ophthalmology.
Lens wearers should keep their lenses and case for culture.
Treated with intensive antibiotic drops (antifungals for fungi).

cmgs.title: Molluscum contagiosum
cmgs.summary: A viral skin infection, mostly in children: pearly spots with a central dimple, which can cause conjunctivitis if on the lid margin.
points: Usually resolves on its own, so watch and wait.
Removal may be advised if lesions are on the lid margin, numerous near the eye, or causing conjunctivitis.

cmgs.title: Nasolacrimal drainage dysfunction
cmgs.summary: A blocked tear duct causing a watery eye. In babies the duct usually opens by itself before 12 months.
points: In adults, syringing with saline or a fluorescein test checks patency, and syringing can sometimes clear it.
Antibiotics if infected.
Refer if it doesn't resolve; surgery creates a new drainage passage.

cmgs.title: Ocular hypertension
cmgs.summary: Consistently raised IOP with no glaucomatous damage. Without treatment about 1 in 10 develop POAG within five years.
points: Refer moderate- or high-risk patients for assessment.
Treatment is SLT laser or pressure-lowering drops.

cmgs.title: Ocular rosacea
cmgs.summary: Rosacea (facial flushing on nose, cheeks, forehead) with eye involvement in about half of cases: blepharitis, tear film problems and, in severe cases, corneal thinning, vessels and scarring.
points: Lid care, lubricants and possibly dietary changes.
Oral tetracyclines help skin and eyes.
Refer if simple measures fail.

cmgs.title: Ophthalmia neonatorum
cmgs.summary: Conjunctivitis in the first 30 days of life, caught from the birth canal. Chlamydia is now the commonest cause; gonorrhoea can damage the cornea.
points: Red, swollen lids with discharge, usually both eyes.
Refer every case immediately for swabs and systemic and topical antibiotics.

cmgs.title: Penetrating injury
cmgs.summary: A sharp object breaks through the cornea or sclera, often at work, during DIY or in an assault; more common in men.
points: Check vision and the extent of the damage, but don't remove an embedded object.
Give pain relief and arrange same-day ophthalmology.
There's a rare risk of sympathetic ophthalmia in the other eye.

cmgs.title: Photokeratitis (arc eye, snow blindness)
cmgs.summary: UV damage to the corneal epithelium from welding, sun lamps or snow glare. Symptoms start 6–12 hours after exposure: pain, redness, watering, photophobia.
points: Resolves on its own without lasting damage.
Comfort drops and oral pain relief.

cmgs.title: Phthiriasis (lash lice)
cmgs.summary: Crab lice on the lashes, usually sexually acquired. Itchy lids, red watery eyes, and nits on the lash bases.
points: Remove lice and nits at the slit lamp.
Explain it's sexually transmitted; partners and family may need checking.
Wash bedding, towels and clothes at 60°C.

cmgs.title: Pigmented fundus lesions
cmgs.summary: Mostly choroidal naevi (like moles), plus harmless CHRPE and, rarely, choroidal melanoma.
points: Check naevi at each routine exam; photograph atypical ones to monitor change.
Suspicious features include size over 4 disc diameters, orange pigment, fluid, thickness and symptoms.
CHRPE needs no monitoring.
cmgs.refer: Suspected melanoma: referral within two weeks.

cmgs.title: Pinguecula
cmgs.summary: A small, raised yellow-white spot at 3 or 9 o'clock beside the cornea, from long-term UV exposure. Common with age; doesn't affect vision.
points: Advise a hat and sunglasses.
Lubricants for irritation; anti-inflammatory drops if inflamed (pingueculitis).
Removal is cosmetic and rarely done on the NHS.

cmgs.title: Post-operative endophthalmitis
cmgs.summary: Infection inside the eye after surgery (under 1 in 1,000 cataract operations), usually from the patient's own skin bacteria. Pain, redness, photophobia, blur and hypopyon.
points: Acute within the first week; chronic up to a month later.
Higher risk in diabetes and immunosuppression.
Treated with intravitreal antibiotics, sometimes vitrectomy.

cmgs.title: Post-operative suture breakage
cmgs.summary: A broken stitch after eye surgery causes a gritty, red, watery, light-sensitive eye.
points: The surgeon trims, removes or replaces it.
cmgs.refer: Urgent or emergency, depending on severity.

cmgs.title: Preseptal and orbital cellulitis
cmgs.summary: Infection of tissues in front of (preseptal) or behind (orbital) the orbital septum, mostly in children under 10, often after sinusitis, a stye or injury.
points: Preseptal is usually mild; orbital can be life-threatening.
Orbital signs: proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements, reduced vision or colour, RAPD.
Most need admission for IV antibiotics with ophthalmology, ENT and paediatrics.
cmgs.refer: Suspected orbital cellulitis: emergency, same day.

cmgs.title: Primary angle closure and angle closure glaucoma
cmgs.summary: A narrow drainage angle: PACS (iris touches the angle, nothing else), PAC (raised IOP or synechiae, healthy nerve) and PACG (with optic nerve damage). More common in women, hyperopes, people of East Asian ancestry and older people.
points: An acute attack gives a painful red eye, blurred vision with haloes, a fixed mid-dilated pupil, very high IOP, nausea and vomiting.
Optometrists can give first-aid drops.
Treated with laser peripheral iridotomy, drugs or lens extraction.
cmgs.refer: Acute attack: emergency, as soon as possible.

cmgs.title: Primary open angle glaucoma
cmgs.summary: Slowly progressive optic nerve damage, usually with raised IOP, from reduced drainage through the trabecular meshwork. Painless and often unnoticed until field is lost.
points: About 2% of over-40s and 4–5% of over-80s in the UK.
Higher risk with family history and African or African-Caribbean ancestry.
Look for disc cupping, typical field defects and IOP (normal in some).
Confirmed cases are managed in hospital with drops or laser (SLT), and surgery if needed.

cmgs.title: Pseudophakic cystoid macular oedema
cmgs.summary: Macular swelling after cataract surgery in 1–2% of patients, peaking at 4–6 weeks. Risk rises with complicated surgery, diabetes or PCMO in the other eye.
points: Reduced or distorted vision; OCT shows cystic spaces.
Mild cases settle; otherwise steroid and NSAID drops.
Refer urgently if there's no improvement after six weeks of treatment.

cmgs.title: Pterygium
cmgs.summary: A triangular wedge of conjunctiva growing onto the cornea, usually nasally, linked to sunlight and dry, dusty conditions.
points: It can induce astigmatism and blur vision.
Measure it to monitor growth.
Lubricants, and short steroid courses if inflamed.
Refer if it advances towards the visual axis or inflammation can't be controlled.

cmgs.title: Recurrent corneal erosion syndrome
cmgs.summary: The corneal epithelium breaks down repeatedly, typically on waking, after an old abrasion or with a corneal dystrophy.
points: Sharp pain, watering and blur on waking.
Lubricating drops and ointment to reduce friction while it heals.
Bandage lens, or referral for minor surgery or laser, if it keeps recurring.

cmgs.title: Retinal vein occlusion
cmgs.summary: A blocked retinal vein (branch, hemi or central) causing sudden painless loss of vision, with haemorrhages and swelling. Linked to age, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, diabetes and glaucoma.
points: Ischaemic types can grow new vessels on the retina or iris, leading to neovascular glaucoma.
Refer urgently to ophthalmology and to the GP for cardiovascular work-up.
Macular oedema is treated with anti-VEGF or steroid injections.
cmgs.refer: Urgent; CRVO with IOP 40 mmHg or more is an emergency.

cmgs.title: Scleritis
cmgs.summary: Severe inflammation of the sclera with deep, boring pain that can wake the patient and spread to the brow or jaw. A third have systemic disease.
points: Anterior (90%) is visibly red; necrotising forms can melt the sclera; posterior scleritis can look normal at the front.
Treated with systemic anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive drugs.

cmgs.title: Seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis
cmgs.summary: Hay fever affecting the eyes (seasonal, mainly grass pollen) or a year-round allergy such as house dust mite (perennial). Itching, redness, watering; sight isn't harmed.
points: Affects about a fifth of adults, often with nasal allergy, asthma or eczema.
Antihistamine or mast-cell-stabiliser drops, and oral antihistamines.

cmgs.title: Steroid-related ocular hypertension and glaucoma
cmgs.summary: Steroids by any route (drops, tablets, injections, implants) can raise IOP in about a third of people, without symptoms.
points: Check IOP in people newly started on steroids.
Stopping the steroid, when safe, usually lets IOP fall; otherwise treat as open angle glaucoma.

cmgs.title: Sub-tarsal foreign body
cmgs.summary: A particle trapped under the upper lid, scratching the cornea on every blink (classically vertical linear staining).
points: Evert the upper lid and remove it, with anaesthetic if needed.
Antibiotics only for a large abrasion or signs of infection.
Rarely needs referral.

cmgs.title: Subconjunctival haemorrhage
cmgs.summary: A painless bright red bleed under the conjunctiva, spontaneous or after minor trauma.
points: Clears in 1–2 weeks without treatment.
Check blood pressure; it's more common with anticoagulants, aspirin and diabetes.
Investigate if it keeps coming back.

cmgs.title: Trichiasis
cmgs.summary: Lashes grow towards the eye, usually from entropion or chronic lid or conjunctival inflammation.
points: Gives a red, uncomfortable, foreign-body feeling and can damage the cornea.
Epilating lashes helps for 4–6 weeks until they regrow; a bandage lens can relieve symptoms.
Persistent cases are referred for electrolysis, cryotherapy, laser or lid surgery.

cmgs.title: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC)
cmgs.summary: A rare, serious allergic disease of young children, mostly boys with eczema or asthma. Intense itching, stringy discharge, light sensitivity, and cobblestone papillae under the upper lid.
points: Usually starts before 10 and often settles at puberty.
Corneal shield ulcers or plaque can damage vision.
Many cases need ophthalmology care.
cmgs.refer: Active limbal or corneal involvement: urgent.

cmgs.title: Vitreomacular traction and macular hole
cmgs.summary: As the vitreous shrinks it can pull on the macula and tear a hole, causing a sudden central blur or distortion in one eye.
points: OCT shows the traction or hole.
Refer: there are no medical treatments.
Surgery is vitrectomy and a gas bubble, which usually improves vision.
